content: These clinical features can be utilized to stratify patients into low-risk or high-risk categories. The presence of multiple high-risk features is directly associated with an increased likelihood of adverse outcomes. Pharmacotherapy: Epinephrine is employed either as a standalone treatment or in combination with surgical techniques to address various causes of lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). Local injection of epinephrine achieves hemostasis through a combination of pressure tamponade and vasoconstriction. In cases of rebleeding, surgical intervention should be considered. Pharmacotherapy is generally used as an adjunctive treatment for all patients with LGIB. Intra-arterial vasopressin infusion halts bleeding in approximately 91% of patients; however, bleeding recurs in up to 50% of cases once the infusion is discontinued. Major Contraindications for Vasopressin Use: Closed-angle glaucoma Active labor Shock Sulfite hypersensitivity Coronary artery disease (CAD) or peripheral artery disease (PAD) Complications of Vasopressin Infusion: Recurrent hemorrhage Myocardial ischemia (which can be managed with a nitroglycerin drip to mitigate cardiac complications) Arrhythmias Hypertension Volume overload with resultant hyponatremia Colonoscopy: Colonoscopy is the preferred initial diagnostic modality for patients presenting with lower gastrointestinal bleeding. It can identify the source of severe LGIB in 74% to 82% of cases. When patients remain hemodynamically stable during bowel preparation and sedation, colonoscopy not only localizes the bleeding source but also allows for therapeutic interventions such as clip placement, epinephrine injection, thermoregulation, or laser photocoagulation. In cases of massive LGIB, colonoscopic hemostasis is an effective method for controlling diverticular bleeding when performed by skilled providers. If no bleeding source is identified during colonoscopy, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) should be performed, as brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) can sometimes present as rectal bleeding due to rapid transit. If bleeding is accompanied by abdominal pain, ischemic bowel disease should be considered. In such cases, computed tomography angiography (CTA) may be a more appropriate first-line investigation, especially if peritonitis is suspected. Timing of Colonoscopy: For patients with ongoing bleeding or high-risk clinical features, colonoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of presentation after adequate bowel preparation to optimize diagnostic and therapeutic outcomes. Bowel Preparation: In patients without active bleeding, rapid bowel preparation can be achieved using 3 to 4 liters of polyethylene glycol, administered either orally or via a nasogastric tube to minimize nausea and reduce the risk of aspiration. However, rapid bowel preparation carries a risk of fluid overload in acutely ill patients. Metoclopramide (10 to 20 mg) can be administered as a prokinetic agent to facilitate gastric emptying and reduce the risk of vomiting during bowel preparation. Some clinicians advocate for limited bowel preparation using polyethylene glycol purges supplemented with rectal enemas. Blood in the colon acts as a cathartic agent, aiding in the evacuation of colonic contents. Complications of Colonoscopy: Perforation of the luminal wall, which can lead to peritonitis and sepsis. Poor visualization in an inadequately prepared colon. Non-Surgical Options: Once the bleeding site is localized, therapeutic options include coagulation and injection with vasoconstrictors or sclerosing agents. For diverticular bleeding, bipolar probe coagulation, epinephrine injection, and metallic clip placement may be utilized. In cases of recurrent bleeding, resection of the affected bowel segment may be necessary. For angiodysplasia, thermal therapies such as electrocautery or argon plasma coagulation are typically effective. Angiodysplastic lesions may be missed during colonoscopy if they are small or obscured by blood clots. Endoscopic hemostasis is a safe and effective method for managing high-risk bleeding indications, such as active bleeding, non-bleeding visible vessels, or adherent clots. It is also effective for diverticular bleeding, angioectasia bleeding, and post-polypectomy bleeding. In patients with brisk, active lower gastrointestinal bleeding, a surgical consultation should be obtained. Diverticula: Diverticula are most commonly found in the descending and sigmoid colon. In most cases, bleeding from diverticulosis resolves spontaneously. However, in approximately 5% of patients, the bleeding can be massive and life-threatening.
